NOUN.title: gender
NOUN.why: Chooses the article (der / die / das), the pronoun and the adjective endings; learned with every noun. Plural-only nouns (class plt) have none.

NOUN.title: plural, per meaning
NOUN.why: The plural is not predictable and is learned with the noun; a meaning may have its own plural (Banken / Bänke) or none (das Land = the countryside). A meaning left out of every item has no plural. none: mass nouns (class sgt) and plural-only nouns (class plt).

NOUN.title: genitive singular
NOUN.why: The genitive singular shows the declension at a glance: des Tisches / des Tischs (-(e)s), des Jungen (n-declension), des Namens (mixed), der Frau (feminine: no ending). Dictionaries give it with the plural (der Tisch, -(e)s, -e). The first form is the usual one. none: plural-only nouns.

NOUN.title: singular declension
NOUN.why: strong: des Tisches, dem Tisch (-(e)s in the genitive); weak (n-declension): den / dem / des Jungen; mixed: des Namens, den Namen; feminine: no ending in the singular; adjectival: declined like an adjective (der Verwandte, ein Verwandter).

NOUN.title: number
NOUN.why: Most nouns have both numbers; mass nouns, months and names of substances are used in the singular only (das Obst, der Reis, die Milch), a few nouns exist only in the plural (die Eltern, die Leute, die Ferien) and have no gender.

NOUN.title: same form, other gender
NOUN.why: der Junge (boy) / das Junge (young animal): the article alone tells two words apart. senses: when the other gender belongs to a meaning of this word.

NOUN.title: clue to the gender
NOUN.why: The rule that gives this noun its gender, when there is one: a suffix (-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ie, -in → die; -chen, -lein, -um → das; -ling → der), a meaning class (days, months, seasons, times of day, male persons → der; female persons → die), the last part of a compound, or the tendency of nouns in -e to be feminine. An exception to a rule says so. none: no rule – the article is learned with the noun.

NOUN.title: female / male counterpart
NOUN.why: Person nouns come in pairs: mostly the feminine is made with -in, often with umlaut (der Lehrer → die Lehrerin, der Arzt → die Ärztin, der Koch → die Köchin); some pairs are different words (der Bruder – die Schwester). form: the counterpart with its article; lexeme: when it is in the lexicon. none: not a person noun, or one noun for everyone (das Kind, die Person).

NOUN.title: diminutive
NOUN.why: -chen (most nouns) or -lein (after -ch, -g, and in literary style) makes a small or endearing thing, usually with umlaut, and is always neuter: das Haus → das Häuschen, das Buch → das Büchlein. Some diminutives are words of their own (das Brötchen = bread roll, das Plätzchen = biscuit). Given when one is in common use; none says why not.

NOUN.title: compound parts
NOUN.why: The last part (head) gives the gender and the plural, the parts before it narrow the meaning; linker = the joining element (Blume-n-kohl, Geburt-s-tag) or “−e” when the first part loses its final e (Kirsch-tomate). A verb as modifier appears as its stem (wohnen → Wohnzimmer). none: a simple or derived word, or two separate words.

NOUN.title: forms of one meaning
NOUN.why: A meaning used in a form or construction of its own besides its plural (Frau as a title: Frau Weber, never plural; Bad in place names: in Bad Ems). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

VERB.title: principal parts
VERB.why: infinitive – 3rd person singular present – 3rd person singular Präteritum – Partizip II: the four forms every learner memorizes (separable verbs with the particle in place: kommt an, kam an, angekommen).

VERB.title: perfect auxiliary
VERB.why: sein for movement and change of state (ist gegangen), haben for the rest; both: it depends on the meaning or on a direct object (hat das Auto gefahren / ist nach Berlin gefahren) – see auxBySense.

VERB.title: auxiliary per meaning
VERB.why: For verbs with aux “both”: which meaning (or construction) takes which auxiliary. none: one auxiliary for every meaning.

VERB.title: vowel change in the present (du / er)
VERB.why: essen → du isst, fahren → du fährst, laufen → du läufst; decides the du-forms and the du-imperative (iss!).

VERB.title: separable particle
VERB.why: The stressed particle goes to the end of the clause (Ich komme morgen an), ge- and zu go inside it (angekommen, anzukommen).

VERB.title: inseparable prefix
VERB.why: An unstressed prefix that never separates and takes no ge- in the participle (verlassen – verlassen).

VERB.title: objects and complements, per meaning
VERB.why: The case of each object (helfen + DAT, kaufen + ACC (+ DAT)), a preposition the verb chooses (warten auf + ACC), or a predicative nominative (Ich heiße Anna). none: the verb takes no object in any meaning.

VERB.title: reflexive use, per meaning
VERB.why: A meaning that needs the reflexive pronoun (sich verlassen auf: ich verlasse mich). none: no reflexive meaning.

VERB.title: conjugation class
VERB.why: weak: -te, ge-…-t (kaufen); strong: vowel change, ge-…-en (trinken – trank – getrunken); mixed: vowel change with weak endings (rennen – rannte – gerannt); modal: modal verbs (mögen, wollen); irregular: sein, haben.

VERB.title: Partizip II: ge- or not
VERB.why: ge- is added when the first syllable is stressed (gekauft, gegangen); after a separable particle it goes inside (aufgewacht, angekommen); verbs with an unstressed prefix (be-, er-, ver- …) and verbs in -ieren take none (besucht, vergessen, reserviert).

VERB.title: imperative (du – ihr – Sie)
VERB.why: The du-form is the stem, -e optional (komm(e)!) but needed after -t, -d (warte!) and -er (erinnere!); verbs with e → i/ie keep the change and never take -e (iss!, lies!), verbs with a → ä do not (fahr!, schlaf!). ihr = the present form (kommt!), Sie = the infinitive + Sie (kommen Sie!). sein: sei! seid! seien Sie!. none: verbs without an imperative (modal verbs).

VERB.title: Konjunktiv II

item.use: enum:common in speech|mostly written|rare (würde + infinitive instead)

VERB.why: The one-word Konjunktiv II (er wäre, hätte, käme, ginge) is common only for sein, haben, werden, the modal verbs and a few frequent strong verbs; for the others it is written style or rare, and speech uses würde + infinitive (er würde essen). none: weak verbs, whose Konjunktiv II is the same as the Präteritum (kaufte) – würde + infinitive is used.

VERB.title: ending adjustments
VERB.why: Stems in -t, -d (and consonant + m/n) insert -e- before -st and -t: du wartest, er wartet, ihr wartet; stems in -s, -ß, -z, -x add only -t in the du-form: du heißt, du reist, du isst; stems in -er / -el take -n (not -en) in the plural forms. none: the endings are added regularly (or the verb is irregular: sein, haben, werden).

VERB.title: past in speech
VERB.why: In speech most verbs tell the past in the Perfekt (ich habe gegessen), the Präteritum being written style; sein, haben, werden and the modal verbs use the Präteritum in speech too (ich war, ich hatte, ich wollte). Northern speakers use the Präteritum more, southern speakers hardly at all.

VERB.title: with another infinitive (Ersatzinfinitiv)
VERB.why: Modal verbs (and lassen, sehen, hören, helfen) in the perfect with a dependent infinitive use their infinitive instead of the Partizip II: Ich habe kommen wollen (not gewollt). none: the Partizip II is always used.

VERB.title: manner of motion
VERB.why: German chooses the verb by how one moves: gehen (on foot), fahren (in a vehicle), fliegen (by air); kommen, reisen say nothing about it.

VERB.title: direction hin / her
VERB.why: hin points away from the speaker, her towards the speaker: Komm herein! (to me) – Geh hinein! (away from me); wohin? – woher?. In speech both often shrink to r- (rein, raus). none: the word marks no direction.

VERB.title: position verb pair
VERB.why: Putting a thing somewhere and its being there are verb pairs by position: stellen – stehen (upright), legen – liegen (lying), setzen – sitzen (sitting), hängen – hängen (hanging). The putting verb is weak and takes the accusative after a two-way preposition, the state verb is strong and takes the dative. none: not one of these verbs.

VERB.title: forms of one meaning
VERB.why: A meaning that uses forms of its own (mögen “would like” → möchte, möchtest …). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

ADJ.title: comparison
ADJ.why: regular: klein – kleiner – am kleinsten; umlaut: alt – älter – am ältesten; irregular: gut – besser – am besten, hoch – höher; not compared: rosa, lila. The forms are in ADJ;CMPR and ADJ;SPRL.

ADJ.title: comparative and superlative
ADJ.why: The comparative and the predicative superlative (am …sten), with umlaut or irregular forms where the adjective has them: alt – älter – am ältesten, gut – besser – am besten. A second form after a slash is also correct. none: the adjective is not compared.

ADJ.title: stem before an ending
ADJ.why: Some adjectives change before an ending: hoch → hoh- (ein hoher Turm), dunkel → dunkl-, teuer → teur-. none: the ending is added to the base form (or the word takes no endings).

ADJ.title: endings
ADJ.why: Before a noun almost every adjective takes endings (ein alter Mann); a few colour words from other languages take none: ein rosa Kleid, eine lila Tasche (colloquially also rosanes, lilanes, oranges – not standard).

ADJ.title: complement, per meaning
ADJ.why: Some adjectives take a complement with a fixed preposition and case (froh über + ACC, hungrig nach + DAT) or a dative of the person who feels something (Mir ist kalt). none: no complement of its own.

ADJ.title: position
ADJ.why: Most adjectives go before a noun (with endings) and after sein / werden (without): das alte Haus – Das Haus ist alt. Ordinals and words like letzte are used before a noun only; a few words only after the verb (Ich bin schuld).

ADV.title: comparative and superlative
ADV.why: Some adverbs compare: oft – öfter – am öftesten, bald – eher – am ehesten. none: not compared (or itself a comparative / superlative form).

ADV.title: direction hin / her
ADV.why: hin points away from the speaker, her towards the speaker: Komm herein! (to me) – Geh hinein! (away from me); wohin? – woher?. In speech both often shrink to r- (rein, raus). none: the word marks no direction.

ADV.title: modal-particle use
ADV.why: Unstressed in the middle of the sentence, a modal particle adds the speaker's attitude, not content: ja (as we know), doch (after all, urging), denn (interest in a question), aber / vielleicht (surprise), nur (urging, wishes), auch (asking for confirmation). function: what it signals, with an example. none: the word has no modal-particle meaning.

ADP.title: case, per meaning
ADP.why: Every preposition decides the case of its noun; the two-way prepositions (in, an, auf …) take the dative for where? and the accusative for where to?, and some meanings take only one (über “about” + ACC, am Montag + DAT). A meaning that is not prepositional (zu “too”, auf “open”) is in no item. A contraction (im, zum) states the case of its article; senses: omitted.

ADP.title: merged with the article
ADP.why: in + dem = im, zu + der = zur; some merged forms are colloquial (unterm, übers). none: no merged forms, or the word is itself a merged form.

ADP.title: da- / wo- form
ADP.why: For a thing (not a person) a preposition with a pronoun becomes da(r)- + preposition, in questions wo(r)- + preposition: darauf / worauf (r before a vowel), damit / womit; colloquially dr- (drauf, drin). Ich warte darauf. Worauf wartest du? none: the preposition has no such form.

ADP.title: position
ADP.why: Most prepositions stand before their noun; a few follow it in some uses (meiner Meinung nach) or always (gegenüber can follow: dem Haus gegenüber).

DET.title: adjective endings after it
DET.why: der-words → weak endings (der gute Wein), ein-words → mixed (ein guter Wein), words that show no case themselves → strong (viel guter Wein, einige gute Freunde).

DET.title: owner
DET.why: The possessive agrees with the owner in its stem (mein / dein / sein / ihr …) and with the thing owned in its ending (mein Bruder, meine Schwester). sein is for a masculine or neuter owner, ihr for a feminine owner and for several owners.

DET.title: addressee
DET.why: dein / euer (du, ihr) or Ihr (Sie). none: the owner is not the person spoken to.

DET.title: standing alone (as a pronoun)
DET.why: Used without a noun, some determiners take forms of their own: ein → einer, eine, ein(e)s; mein → meiner, meine, mein(e)s; der → dessen, deren, denen in the genitive and dative plural. none: the same forms as before a noun.

DET.title: stem before an ending
DET.why: euer drops its e before an ending (eure, euren), unser may do so in literary style (unsre). none: the endings are added to the base form, or the word takes no endings.

DET.title: forms of one meaning
DET.why: A meaning with forms of its own (ein standing alone → einer, eine, eins). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

PRON.title: what it refers to
PRON.why: er / sie / es refer to things as well, by the gender of the noun (der Tisch → er); wer asks for persons, was for things.

PRON.title: addressee
PRON.why: du / ihr (informal) or Sie (formal). none: not a pronoun of address.

PRON.title: possessive
PRON.why: The possessive determiner that belongs to the pronoun: ich → mein, er / es → sein, sie → ihr, Sie → Ihr. none: no possessive of its own.

PRON.title: reflexive form
PRON.why: The pronoun used when the object is the subject itself: mich / mir, dich / dir, uns, euch – and sich for every third person and for Sie (ich wasche mich, er wäscht sich, Sie waschen sich).

PRON.title: forms of one meaning
PRON.why: A meaning with forms of its own (das Ich, die Ichs; Ihr written with a capital). none: every meaning uses the same forms.

NUM.title: ordinal (der …)
NUM.why: The ordinal adjective: -te up to 19 (der zweite), -ste from 20 (der zwanzigste); irregular erste, dritte, siebte (also siebente), achte.

NUM.title: in longer numerals
NUM.why: Numerals are written as one word up to a million, units before tens joined by und (einundzwanzig, zweihundertvierunddreißig); some numbers change in compounds (sechs → sechzehn, sechzig; sieben → siebzehn, siebzig; drei → dreißig). none: the form is unchanged in compounds, or the word is itself a compound.

SCONJ.title: position of the finite verb
values: at the end of its clause
SCONJ.why: A subordinating conjunction sends the finite verb to the end of its clause (…, weil ich Hunger habe).

CCONJ.title: effect on word order
CCONJ.why: und, oder, aber, denn stand before the clause and change nothing (…, denn ich habe Hunger); weder / noch take the first place, so the verb follows them (Weder hat er angerufen, noch …).

CCONJ.title: paired form
CCONJ.why: Two-part conjunctions: weder … noch (neither … nor), entweder … oder (either … or), zwar … aber (admittedly … but), sowohl … als auch (both … and). none: not part of a pair.

CCONJ.title: modal-particle use
CCONJ.why: Unstressed in the middle of the sentence, a modal particle adds the speaker's attitude, not content: ja (as we know), doch (after all, urging), denn (interest in a question), aber / vielleicht (surprise), nur (urging, wishes), auch (asking for confirmation). function: what it signals, with an example. none: the word has no modal-particle meaning.

INTJ.title: formality
INTJ.why: Which situations the formula fits: informal (friends, family: hallo, tschüss), formal (strangers, customers: guten Tag, auf Wiedersehen, wie geht es Ihnen), neutral (both).

INTJ.title: usual reply
INTJ.why: Formulas come with their answer: danke – bitte, wie geht's? – gut, danke, und dir?. none: the word is itself an answer.

INTJ.title: region
INTJ.why: Where the formula is used, and what other German-speaking regions say instead (Grüß Gott in southern Germany and Austria, Moin in the north, Grüezi in Switzerland). none: used everywhere, with no common regional alternative.

INTJ.title: modal-particle use
INTJ.why: Unstressed in the middle of the sentence, a modal particle adds the speaker's attitude, not content: ja (as we know), doch (after all, urging), denn (interest in a question), aber / vielleicht (surprise), nur (urging, wishes), auch (asking for confirmation). function: what it signals, with an example. none: the word has no modal-particle meaning.

PART.title: modal-particle use
PART.why: Unstressed in the middle of the sentence, a modal particle adds the speaker's attitude, not content: ja (as we know), doch (after all, urging), denn (interest in a question), aber / vielleicht (surprise), nur (urging, wishes), auch (asking for confirmation). function: what it signals, with an example. none: the word has no modal-particle meaning.
